<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
The comment's core corrections are well documented and mostly hold up. The attrition finding is the most damaging new fact about the Halden pilot. But the conclusion goes far beyond the evidence. Its central claim, that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact", is contradicted by evidence the comment itself cites. It also judges competing explanations by different standards, and its abstract describes a correction that was never made.

## Arithmetic checks

**These pass:**
- Hours: 34.6/40.3 = 0.859 (−14.1%) and 34.8/40.4 = 0.861 (−13.9%).
- Table 2: 95.1/0.8 = +18.9%, 98.4/0.859 = +14.6%, 95.4/0.861 = +10.8%.
- Real revenue: 1.014/1.041 = −2.6%.
- Hours overstatement: 20% − 14.1% = 5.9 points.

**These don't:**
- **The hours decomposition doesn't add up.** Section 3 attributes the shortfall to +0.7 hours a day on four days (+2.8 hours) plus 1.6 hours on the day off, so +4.4 hours over the 32 scheduled, about 36.4 a week. Reported actual hours are 34.6, only +2.6. Either the components are averaged over different groups (e.g. the 1.6 hours applies only to staff who worked the day off), or one figure is wrong. It needs reconciling.
- **The energy extrapolation is off.** Energy fell from +0.61 SD to +0.29 SD over three months, about 0.107 SD a month. A linear trend reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten". It's a minor slip, but two data points can't support a linear extrapolation anyway.

## What the comment gets right

- **Attrition.** If seven of the nine withdrawals happened *after* the schedule began, mostly over workload, the Halden paper's "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons" is a material misreport. It is the most important new fact here.
- **Manager vs record-based output.** Managers' figures exceeded the records in 19 of 23 organisations. A one-sided sign test gives p ≈ 0.001, so the bias is unlikely to be chance. The comment could report this to strengthen its case.
- **The hours denominator, the per-hour artifact at 80, and nominal revenue** are correct. The Halden working paper should address all of them.
- **The recommendations** in Section 8 are sound.

## Major problems

### 1. The conclusion is contradicted by evidence the comment itself cites

The comment calls the Varden counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature". The case-processing stratum of the same trial is at least as reliable: more offices, randomised, record-based output, timesheet hours, nine months long. It found output per actual hour up 12.5% (CI +6.9 to +18.4). That design rules out the three artifacts the comment names:

- **Selection** is removed by randomisation.
- **Measurement** is addressed by administrative output records and timesheet hours.
- **Novelty** is at least partly addressed by the longer duration and the control offices, who also knew a trial was under way.

The comment never mentions this result. Citing one stratum of a trial as the most reliable evidence while omitting the other stratum is selective. Any claim that gains are "entirely an artifact" has to engage with it.

### 2. The abstract says attrition was corrected; it wasn't

The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems (attrition, output measure, hours) reduces the gain to 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is described but never quantified.

The comment has the withdrawals' exit data and presumably some outcome or employee data. It could estimate bounds, such as worst-case imputation or Lee bounds. For example: what is the pooled gain if the nine withdrawals are assigned zero per-hour gain, or record-based output equal to the lowest observed? Without this, "attrition accounts for part of the gain" is a plausible claim, not a demonstrated one.

### 3. Table 2 compares different samples and reports no uncertainty

- **Different samples.** The four rows use 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. Moving between rows changes the sample as well as the correction, so the table doesn't isolate the effect of each correction. The fix is to compute every specification within the same 17 organisations, starting from their manager index and scheduled hours. That would show how much each correction contributes for a fixed group.
- **No confidence intervals anywhere.** With 17 organisations, the 10.8% estimate is likely imprecise. The comment criticises the original for presenting point estimates as findings but does the same.
- **Weighting isn't stated.** Halden used employee-weighted means. If these are unweighted, the comparison with 23.4% isn't like-for-like.
- **Unrepresentative subset.** The Data note concedes the subsets aren't random. Organisations with time tracking and billable or ticket records are probably concentrated in professional services and software. The 10.8% then mostly describes those sectors, which conflicts with using it to dismiss gains generally.

### 4. The novelty argument is untested, and the test is available

The comment has microdata with a **monthly** output index. If novelty drives the residual gain, output (or output per hour) should decline from around month three to month six, mirroring the energy measure. The comment doesn't check.

Instead it infers a productivity trajectory from a self-reported energy score, which is a different construct, using two time points. If the monthly output series shows the same decay, the novelty claim becomes much stronger. If it is flat, the claim fails. Either way, the analysis should be run before the conclusion is drawn.

### 5. Competing explanations are held to different standards

- **Meetings.** This explanation is dismissed as a post hoc account resting on seven offices.
- **Novelty.** This explanation is accepted, though it rests on two survey time points, wasn't pre-specified, and isn't tested against output.

The two hypotheses are roughly comparable in evidential strength, so they should be judged by the same standard.

The meetings critique also misdescribes the Varden analysis:
- **Not a selected subgroup.** The seven offices are all of the treated case-processing offices, a pre-registered stratum.
- **Not collected after the results.** The calendar data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results.
- **Caveats already stated.** The Varden authors flagged that the analysis was unregistered, warned that seven offices cannot establish a mechanism, and registered a confirmatory test.

The comment's caution is fair, but it adds little to what Varden already said. "Should not be cited as a mechanism" is reasonable. "A post hoc account fitted to a subgroup" is not accurate.

### 6. "Not proven" has become "proven false"

Section 6 argues, reasonably, that six months can't distinguish novelty from a durable effect and that the burden of proof lies with those claiming durability. That supports "the durable gain is unestablished". It does not support "the gains are *entirely* an artifact", which is a positive claim of zero effect. Even within the comment's own analysis, a gain of about 11% survives correction and is explained away only by the untested novelty hypothesis. The generalisation from one pilot to "reduced-hours schemes" in general also goes beyond what one re-analysis can support.

## Minor points

- **Deflator.** CPI isn't the ideal deflator for business revenue. Producer or service-sector output prices would be better. The direction of the correction is probably right, but the size may differ.
- **Records aren't a gold standard.** "Billable hours delivered" is partly an input measure, so it mechanically falls when hours fall. Ticket and unit counts don't capture quality. The manager–record gap is still telling, but some of it may reflect what the records miss.
- **Retail figure.** The 11.2% retail and hospitality fall rests on three organisations. Say so in the text.
- **Varden counter stratum.** Calling it "the most reliable finding" ignores its known caveats: 5 vs 5 offices, few-cluster inference, and possible call pooling between centres. Its result also reflects a design with no added staff. "Reduced hours reduce output where output depends on presence" should add "without added staffing".
- **The ninth withdrawal.** Six withdrawals gave workload reasons and two gave scheduling. The ninth's reason isn't stated.

## Suggested reframing of the conclusion

Something like this would be defensible: correcting for record-based output and actual hours cuts the reported per-hour gain by more than half, to about 11% in the subset where both are available. Non-random attrition after the schedule began probably biases even this figure upward. Whether the remaining gain persists is untested. The best randomised evidence shows a per-hour gain of similar size in case-processing work at nine months, and a loss of output per employee in coverage-bound work without added staff.

That keeps the comment's real contributions and drops claims it can't support.

I can draft a reply-to-comment from the Halden authors' perspective, or a referee report on the comment, if either would help.
